name: Djenné
info: Djenné is a town in the Inland Niger Delta of central Mali, on the floodplain between the Niger and Bani rivers, grown from an urban settlement first occupied around 200 BCE into a trading and Islamic learning centre linked to Timbuktu.

facts.founded: The nearby site of Djenné-Djeno was first settled around 200 BCE according to excavations of 1977 and 1981; the present town was first settled after 1000 CE, while oral tradition dates its founding to 635 and names a legendary founder, Maafir.
facts.where: On the floodplain between the Niger and Bani rivers at the southern end of the Inland Niger Delta in central Mali, 398 km north-east of Bamako and 76 km south-west of Mopti.
facts.known: The old site of Djenné-Djeno; the trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves; Islamic scholarship beside Timbuktu; the Songhai siege of 1471; the Moroccan conquest; adobe architecture; the Great Mosque
facts.today: Djenné is a town and urban commune of the Mopti Region of Mali and, with Djenné-Djeno, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.

t: Djenné grew from the older urban settlement of Djenné-Djeno, first occupied around 200 BCE, and the present town, settled after 1000 CE, took over as the older site was abandoned by about 1400.

Between the 15th and 17th centuries much of the trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves that passed through Timbuktu also passed through Djenné, and both towns were centres of Islamic scholarship.
Sonni Ali took the town in 1471, Moroccan forces held the region after 1591, and later it passed to the Segou kingdom, the Massina Empire, the Toucouleur Empire and, in 1893, France.
dyk: Each year the floods of the Bani and Niger rivers turn Djenné into an island, reached by causeways. Its mud-brick houses must be replastered at least every other year, and the Great Mosque every year.
ev: The present town of Djenné is first settled
Sonni Ali conquers Djenné after a siege of about six months
The Songhai are defeated at Tondibi by a Moroccan army, and their empire collapses
Djenné becomes part of the Segou kingdom
René Caillié becomes the first European to visit the town
French forces under Louis Archinard occupy Djenné
UNESCO names Djenné and Djenné-Djeno a World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
Djenné stands on the floodplain between the Niger and Bani rivers at the southern end of the Inland Niger Delta, in central Mali. The town covers about 70 ha, and in the annual flood, which begins in July and reaches its maximum in October, it becomes an island reached by causeways. The earliest urban settlement lay 2.5 km to the south-east, at Djenné-Djeno, meaning 'old Djenne'. Excavations by Susan and Roderick McIntosh in 1977 and 1981 indicate that it was first settled around 200 BCE. The town itself was then called Djoboro, and one account holds that Soninke immigrants from the Wagadou region founded it during an increasingly dry period that made the Inner Niger Delta more habitable.

Oral traditions recount a legendary founder named Maafir, who came from Yemen and was descended from Esau. They also say that the town was founded in 635 around the home of a powerful djinn, Shamharoush, who had been blessed by the prophet Muhammad; these traditions do not distinguish between Djenné and Djoboro. Preliminary excavations within modern Djenné indicate that the present town was first settled after 1000 CE. Its name derives from jannah, the Islamic paradise. In legend Tapama Djenepo was sacrificed on the founding of the city, and a tomb in the town is attributed to her.
sections.growth:
Djoboro developed into a large walled urban complex between 300 and 850 CE. The city and its environs, including the later site of Djenné, are estimated to have had from 10,000 to 26,000 inhabitants in 800 CE. After 1100 the population of Djenné-Djeno declined and by 1400 the site had been abandoned, as were many smaller settlements within a few kilometres of it. The cause of this collapse is unknown, but it may have included new diseases arriving through trans-Saharan trade, or warfare. Djenné itself remained fully occupied and survived as a centre of regional trade.

Between the 15th and 17th centuries much of the trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves that moved in and out of Timbuktu passed through Djenné. Salt mined at Taghaza in the Sahara travelled south through Timbuktu and Djenné, and gold from the Akan goldfields, traded at Begho, travelled north through them to North Africa, where it was exchanged for cloth, copper and brass. Under the Songhai the town had a population of approximately 40,000. Between the 14th and 17th centuries Djenné and Timbuktu were also important centres of Islamic study. The town's prosperity depended on this trade, and when the Portuguese established trading posts on the African coast and shipped gold from Elmina, the importance of the trans-Saharan trade, and so of Djenné, declined.
sections.rulers:
Djoboro was ruled by 25 chiefs before the coming of Islam in the late 600s, although Siigha, the first Muslim ruler, is presumably mythical. Djenné had a complicated relationship with the Mali Empire, which rose to power in the 13th century. The two major 17th-century chronicles disagree: al-Sadi claims that the Malians attacked the town ninety-nine times but never conquered it, while the Tarikh al-fattash describes the chief of Djenné as a humble vassal of the Malian emperor. Djenné was probably a tribute-paying, sometimes vassal city-state.

In 1471 Sonni Ali of the Songhai Empire conquered the town soon after taking Timbuktu. The siege lasted approximately six months. The sultan died during it, his young son made peace, and his mother married Sonni Ali, which established the city's high political position within the empire. Under the Songhai the city was led by the Jenne-koi, or king, and a Jenne-mondio, who answered to the Askias, collected taxes and customs duties. After the Moroccan victory at Tondibi in 1591 the Saadians held the region, but by 1630 they had lost control. Djenné then changed hands several times. It formed part of the Segou kingdom from 1670 to 1818 and of the Massina Empire of the Fulani ruler Seku Amadu from 1818 to 1861. In 1861 it became part of the Toucouleur Empire under Umar Tall, and in April 1893 French forces under Louis Archinard occupied it. The French chose Mopti as the regional capital.
sections.life:
Djenné was a centre of Islamic scholarship, and its Quranic schools still attract students from outside the region. In 1828 René Caillié, who travelled disguised as a Muslim, described a town about two and a half miles in circumference, surrounded by an earth wall about ten feet high. Its houses were built of sun-dried bricks, mostly of one storey, terraced and without external windows, with the rooms lit from an inner court, and the slaves cooked in the open air. Leo Africanus, who may not have seen the town himself, described a village of clay houses with straw roofs, with barley, rice, livestock, fish and cotton, and merchants who visited Timbuktu in small canoes during the annual flood.

The traditional flat-roofed two-storey houses are built around a small central courtyard, with pilaster-like buttresses and pinnacles above the entrance door. Their façades carry bundles of rônier palm sticks, called toron, which project about 60 cm and serve as ready-made scaffolding. The bricks are made on the river bank from earth and chopped straw, and the walls are plastered with earth and rice husks. Houses built before 1900 include some in the Toucouleur style, with a covered entrance porch between two buttresses. The inhabitants mostly speak a Songhay variety, Djenné Chiini, and the surrounding villages speak Bozo, Fulfulde or Bambara. The Maiga family supplies the town's traditional chief.
sections.crises:
The decline of Djenné-Djeno after 1100 and its abandonment by 1400 have no known cause. In 1471 Sonni Ali besieged Djenné for about six months. The flooding of the Bani protected the city but also allowed his river fleet to blockade it. In the 16th century the Portuguese trading posts on the coast shipped large quantities of gold from Elmina, and this maritime trade competed with the trans-Saharan gold trade.

The Songhai collapsed after the Battle of Tondibi in 1591, when a Moroccan army of 4,000 mercenaries led by Judar Pasha, sent by Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur, defeated them. In 1599 the Mali Empire attempted to fill the void but was defeated by the Moroccans outside the walls of Djenné. The Saadians could not control so distant a territory and had lost it by 1630. The collapse of a centralised kingdom able to maintain order over a wide area led to a lack of security and a decline in the movement of traders and scholars. Under French rule the choice of Mopti as regional capital reduced the town's importance, and in the 20th century its commerce declined because of its relatively isolated position. Drought in the 1970s reduced the flow of the Niger and Bani rivers and caused great hardship in the already impoverished town.
sections.legacy:
Djenné is known for its Sudanese-style architecture, and nearly all its buildings, the Great Mosque included, are made of sun-baked earthen bricks coated with plaster. The French journalist Félix Dubois visited in 1895, and his book and its French edition of 1897 made Djenné and its architecture known in Europe and the United States. The French colonial administration arranged for the present Great Mosque to be built in the early 20th century on the site of an earlier mosque. Dubois, revisiting in 1910, was horrified by what he took to be a French design with three minarets like bell towers, while Jean-Louis Bourgeois has argued that the design is basically African. The mosque is replastered every year, and one of its minarets collapsed in 2009 after heavy rain.

The Old Towns of Djenné comprise four archaeological sites, Djenné-Djeno, Hambarkétolo, Kaniana and Tonomba, and UNESCO named them a World Heritage Site in 1988. A survey of 1984 identified 134 two-storey buildings of significant architectural importance, but by 1995 30% of them had been demolished and mostly replaced by new adobe buildings. From 1996 to 2003 the Dutch government funded the restoration of around 100 older buildings. Djenné is today the administrative centre of the Djenné Cercle in the Mopti Region, and its commune had a population of 32,944 in 2009. Its economy rests mainly on agriculture, fishing and livestock.

summary: Djenné, in the Inland Niger Delta of central Mali, grew beside the older site of Djenné-Djeno and became a trading and Islamic learning centre linked to Timbuktu. Songhai, Moroccan, Segou, Massina, Toucouleur and French rulers followed one another there. It is known for its adobe architecture.

notes: START: Djenné-Djeno first settled around 200 BCE (article, McIntosh excavations); the article also says the site was important 'from the 3rd century BC' in the Sights section. The present town is dated after 1000 CE; the tradition says 635. I used -200, circa true.
GREAT MOSQUE DATE: the lead says built in 1907; the Great Mosque section says 1906 (arranged by the colonial administration). Left the year out of the text and used 'early 20th century'.
DROUGHT DATE: the article says early 1970s (annual flood section) and late 1970s (economy). Text says 'in the 1970s'.
Mali Empire: the two chronicles conflict (al-Sadi vs Tarikh al-fattash); stated as a disagreement, as the article states it.
1471 siege: the article's sentence 'blockading the city until.' is garbled; I left out what the blockade ended with. The 'sultan' who died is not named.

Population: 10,000 to 26,000 in 800 CE (for the city and environs, including the later site of Djenne) and about 40,000 under the Songhai are as the article gives them; the Songhai figure is undated. The 2009 figure is for the commune, which includes ten villages.

Leo Africanus: the article says scholars suggest his account was not first-hand; hedged. 'The Maiga family supplies the town's traditional chief' is from the Sights section. The tomb of Tapama Djenepo is attributed in legend.
Left out: tourism, hotels, dams, climate figures, aid projects other than the Dutch restoration, wastewater project, Pacheco Pereira and Barros quotations, the Aga Khan Trust.
Songhai and the Askia: 'Djenne did not support Askia Muhammad I when he rebelled against Sonni Baru, but quickly acquiesced' omitted for space.
